Time Management In Performance; Series 6 Knowing When to Hold, Flow, Adapt and Let Go. Series 6 — Read the Room Without Losing the Plan A good performer watches more than the clock. You should also watch the room. Is the audience engaged? Are they becoming restless? Has a particular section created an emotional response? Is the energy building or declining? This is particularly important for singers, worship teams, choirs, bands and music directors. For example, a choir may have planned a five-minute transition between two songs. During the first song, the congregation becomes deeply engaged. Continuing exactly as rehearsed may interrupt the atmosphere. The director may shorten the transition and move naturally into the next section. Conversely, a band may be performing an energetic number and notice that the audience has not connected with the extended instrumental section. The leader can bring the section to its planned ending rather than stretching it simply because the musicians are enjoying themselves. Reading the room does not mean becoming controlled by audience reaction. It means being aware enough to make informed decisions. As a mentor, I encourage performers to develop this awareness alongside musical skill. Great performers don’t merely play at an audience.
